title: Cook Ding Carves the Ox
text:
Cook Ding was cutting up an ox for Lord Wenhui. Every movement of his hand, every push of his shoulder, every step and every press of his knee was in rhythm, and his knife slid through with a sound like music, as if he were performing an ancient dance. Lord Wenhui was amazed and praised his skill.

Cook Ding put down his knife and said that what he cared about was the Way, which goes beyond skill. When he first began cutting up oxen, all he could see was the whole ox. After three years, he no longer saw the whole ox. Now he met it with his spirit rather than his eyes. He followed the natural structure, slipping his blade through the big gaps and along the hollows, never touching a ligament, let alone a bone.

A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it once a month, because he hacks. Ding had used his knife for nineteen years and cut up thousands of oxen, and its edge was as fresh as if it had just come from the whetstone. Still, whenever he came to a difficult knot, he slowed down, looked carefully, and moved his blade very lightly until the meat fell apart like a clod of earth.

Lord Wenhui said that, hearing the cook, he had learned how to care for life.
lesson: Study the structure of a problem until you can work along its natural joints. Effort spent fighting the grain wears you out; effort that follows it lasts for years.
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 3 (The Secret of Caring for Life)
